task.name: company_research
task.description: A sourced one-page briefing on a company, for meeting or interview prep.
task.system:
You are a research analyst preparing a briefing for someone about to meet this company.
Be specific and current. Cite a source for every factual claim. If you can't find
something, say so rather than guessing.
task.user:
Write a briefing on OpenRouter with these sections:
1. What they do, who buys it, and how they make money
2. Recent news and launches (last 6 months)
3. Funding, size, and financial signals
4. Leadership
5. Main competitors and how they differ
6. Likely strategic priorities and open questions
Keep it under 500 words.

rubric.name: grounding
rubric.description: Factual claims are supported by the cited sources; nothing invented or unsupported.

rubric.name: specificity
rubric.description: Concrete facts (names, numbers, dates, products) rather than generic statements.

rubric.name: recency
rubric.description: Reflects current information, not stale or outdated facts.

rubric.name: usefulness
rubric.description: Would genuinely prepare someone for a meeting; strategic section shows real insight. Length is not a virtue.

rationales: A concrete, timely briefing that distinguishes estimates from company figures and flags conflicting metrics, though several product, pricing, and deal details exceed its supplied excerpts.

B covers all six sections with useful facts, but overstates the deal’s status, introduces unsupported customers, and presents conflicting token-volume figures without explanation.
The briefing uses a strong source for the acquisition and offers useful strategic questions, but several commercial and leadership details are unsupported, and it exceeds the requested length.

# OpenRouter Briefing (as of Oct 12, 2026)

## 1. What they do, who buys, how they earn
OpenRouter is a unified API and marketplace for LLMs. It started in early 2023 and claims 500+ models, 80+ providers and 10M+ users ([openrouter.ai](https://openrouter.ai/about)). Developers buy credits, call one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and get automatic failover across providers ([openrouter.ai](https://openrouter.ai/blog/insights/openrouter-vs-portkey/)). Buyers include individual developers and, increasingly, enterprises that want spend controls and cheaper models for easier tasks ([menlovc.com](https://menlovc.com/perspective/openrouter-now-processes-more-than-a-quadrillion-tokens-a-year/)).

**Revenue:** Provider pricing passes through at 0% markup. OpenRouter charges a 5.5% fee on credit purchases ($0.80 minimum) and 5% on bring-your-own-key usage ([openrouter.ai](https://openrouter.ai/blog/insights/openrouter-vs-portkey/)).

## 2. Recent news
- **Stripe acquisition:** Announced Aug 19, 2026. Stripe is paying $7.5B, per a person familiar with the deal: $1.5B to founders and $6B to investors ([nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/19/business/stripe-openrouter-ai.html)). I found no source on closing status.
- **Usage shift:** Chinese open-source models have grown to 50%+ of usage, led by DeepSeek, Tencent, Xiaomi and Z.ai ([sacra.com](https://sacra.com/research/openrouter-growing-29-mom-at-140m-year/)).
- **Product direction:** Multimodal models (image, audio, embeddings, video), OpenRouter Enterprise, and smarter routing ([menlovc.com](https://menlovc.com/perspective/openrouter-now-processes-more-than-a-quadrillion-tokens-a-year/)).

## 3. Funding, size, financials
- **Funding:** $40M from Menlo about a year before its post, then a $113M Series B at a $1.3B valuation led by CapitalG ([menlovc.com](https://menlovc.com/perspective/openrouter-now-processes-more-than-a-quadrillion-tokens-a-year/)).
- **Team:** About 50 people, per the same Menlo post.
- **Revenue:** Sacra estimates $140M annualized in July 2026, growing 29% MoM over four months. Per-token monetization has fallen ~60% as cheaper tokens dominate ([sacra.com](https://sacra.com/research/openrouter-growing-29-mom-at-140m-year/)). These are third-party estimates, not company-reported.
- **Data conflicts:** Token volume figures differ by source: ~250T/month (Sacra), 600T+/month (OpenRouter's own page), and a ~1.5 quadrillion/year run rate (Menlo, undated). Sacra also cited a ~$10B reported price, while the NYT reports $7.5B. The NYT figure is later and reflects the announced deal. Ask which metrics they use.

## 4. Leadership
- **Alex Atallah:** Founder, previously started OpenSea ([menlovc.com](https://menlovc.com/perspective/openrouter-now-processes-more-than-a-quadrillion-tokens-a-year/)). The NYT describes him as "a founder" ([nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/19/business/stripe-openrouter-ai.html)).
- **Chris Clark:** COO, previously a two-time founder ([menlovc.com](https://menlovc.com/perspective/openrouter-now-processes-more-than-a-quadrillion-tokens-a-year/)).
- **Not found:** Formal CEO title and other executives. Also unknown is how leadership roles change under Stripe.

## 5. Competitors
Sacra describes the category as split into wholesale token marketplaces (OpenRouter), public gateways (Vercel), and behind-the-firewall options (Kong) ([sacra.com](https://sacra.com/research/openrouter-growing-29-mom-at-140m-year/)). Model routing is also becoming a built-in feature in Cursor, Databricks and Ramp (same source).
- **Portkey:** A governance and observability control plane that sits over keys you already hold. It is now part of Palo Alto Networks. OpenRouter owns the path to the model and holds the provider relationships ([openrouter.ai](https://openrouter.ai/blog/insights/openrouter-vs-portkey/)).

## 6. Strategic priorities and open questions
**Likely priorities (inferred from the sources):**
- Integrating with Stripe, pairing routing with usage-based billing. Sacra points to Stripe's Metronome acquisition.
- Enterprise spend management.
- Multimodal expansion.
- Intelligent routing.

**Questions to ask:**
- Does the deal close, and how independent will OpenRouter stay, including neutrality toward providers?
- How will margins hold as the per-token fee base shrinks?
- How exposed is the business to Chinese open-source models, now over half of usage?
- Will bundled routing from platforms like Vercel, Cursor and Databricks erode demand?

citations.title: OpenRouter vs Portkey: Routing Network vs Control Plane
citations.content:
OpenRouter is a managed routing network. You buy credits, call one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and it routes across 70+ providers with automatic failover. You never hold a provider key. Portkey is an AI control plane, now part of Palo Alto Networks after a 2026 acquisition. It sits in front of the provider keys you already have and adds governance, prompt management, guardrails, and observability.

...

Pick OpenRouter when you want model access and failover with no infrastructure. Pick Portkey when you need a governance layer over the provider accounts you already run.

...

OpenRouter owns the path to the model. Your app calls `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`, OpenRouter picks a provider, and forwards the request on credits you’ve already bought. There are no per-provider accounts to manage, and a request that fails on one provider falls over to another automatically.

...

Portkey’s count is breadth of models you can address once you’ve supplied the keys. OpenRouter’s count is models it actively routes to, with credits, load balancing, and cross-provider failover handled for you. Its Auto Router, powered by the wisdom of the market, classifies each prompt and ranks candidates by the aggregate spend of the OpenRouter community over a trailing 7-day window for that task type, and provider routing lets you filter by price, throughput, latency, data policy, and quantization.

...

The two price along different axes. OpenRouter passes provider pricing through at 0% markup, then charges a 5.5% platform fee on credit purchases with a $0.80 minimum. Bring Your Own Key has a 5% fee on equivalent OpenRouter cost after a plan-dependent free allowance; see the pricing page for current details. You pay for usage, nothing else.

...

Net cost depends on where your weight sits. Heavy model spend with provider keys already in hand often favors Portkey’s self-hosted gateway; usage you’d rather not meter or operate favors OpenRouter’s pay-as-you-go.

...

These aren’t mutually exclusive. You can point Portkey at OpenRouter as an upstream provider, putting Portkey’s governance and prompt management in front of OpenRouter’s routing network. OpenRouter also lists Portkey as an upcoming broadcast destination, so traces will flow the other direction too.

citations.content:
When we announced our $40M investment in OpenRouter almost exactly one year ago, they had 2.5M+ developers and had just crossed a ~100 trillion tokens/year run rate. Today, they are at 8M+ developers and, as of this week, will be at a ~1.5 quadrillion tokens/year run rate. That’s one followed by 15 zeros. For comparison, that’s ~15-30% of all of Google’s token run rate, 20-40% of OpenAI’s run rate, and likely >50% of Azure Foundry. On the back of this growth, they’ve raised a $113M Series B at a $1.3B valuation led by CapitalG. Their revenue has already doubled since the round was done in February.

...

### What is OpenRouter? 

OpenRouter helps developers and organizations access, route, and choose inference across 400+ AI models through one unified interface.

...

OpenRouter is a lean team of ~50 people. That’s over 20 trillion tokens per year per employee and ~$2M in net revenue per employee. This isn’t the founders’ first rodeo either: Alex Atallah is a 3x founder who previously started the $13B NFT company OpenSea, and COO Chris Clark is a 2x former founder of a public company. The team is remote-friendly with a cluster of employees in NYC and prioritizes startup experience over pedigree, with most of its engineers coming from places where they’ve actually built things from 0 to 1. Compared to many startups, OpenRouter is actually quite fairly valued, especially given the velocity of its growth since the last round already. They’re positioned so squarely in the middle of the AI stack that there’s a lot of headroom to grow in many different directions.

...

The main things that OpenRouter has been working on in the last year are:

...

- Going beyond text models. Going multimodal. You can now get image, audio (speech and transcription), embedding, and video models on OR. This area continues to be something the team is working on in the coming year.
- Going enterprise. Businesses are overspending on AI, and companies like Uber and Microsoft are blowing through their token budgets. OpenRouter Enterprise allows you to bring all models to the enterprise, set spend management rules, and allow your employees to use cheaper models for easier tasks, too, while boosting your uptime (and not sacrificing on the capacity you have already)
- Intelligent routing. OpenRouter does already support automatic request routing from prompts today. But routing based on just the current prompt isn’t quite good enough for production. Soon, enterprises on OpenRouter will be able to use its observability to automatically find callsites where they could’ve just used a cheaper model and got the same quality. After all, routing is in the name.

citations.content:
LiteLLM: Founded in 2023 out of Y Combinator’s Winter 2023 batch, LiteLLM has raised $1.6 million in total funding as of August 2026. It provides an open-source Python SDK and a self-hosted proxy server that normalizes requests and responses across 100+ model APIs into the OpenAI format, letting engineering teams call any model API without worrying about each model's different syntax. Beyond normalization, teams can define their own routing logic to determine how calls are distributed across different models.

...

OpenRouter takes a fundamentally different approach. It is a cloud-hosted API that developers call externally. A single API call goes to OpenRouter’s endpoint, and its routing intelligence directs the request to the best-fit model across hundreds of models and 80+ providers based on price, performance, and availability. There is no configuration, no infrastructure to manage, and no proxy to run.

...

This distinction drives every other difference

...

OpenRouter offers a free plan, a usage-based plan, and an enterprise plan. The free plan carries no platform fees, but access is limited to 25 models and four providers. It also excludes auto-routing, preferred vendor selections, budget and spend controls, prompt caching, and admin controls. The usage-based plan charges a 5.5% platform fee on all inference spend and unlocks the full platform: the full model catalog, all providers, auto-routing, preferred vendor selections, budget and spend controls, prompt caching, and admin controls. The enterprise plan includes everything in usage-based, layering on enterprise security and governance features, including managed policy enforcement, Provider Data Explorer, single sign-on (SSO), and contractual service-level agreements (SLAs).

...

The free plan may serve as a natural acquisition channel, giving developers hands-on access to the platform before converting to usage-based as their inference needs grow. The usage-based plan is where OpenRouter monetizes. The 5.5% fee on inference spend means revenue scales directly with the volume of tokens processed through the platform, aligning OpenRouter’s incentives with its users. The platform earns more only if developers route more calls through it, so OpenRouter has an incentive to consistently offer the broadest model selection, the most reliable uptime, and the most intelligent routing.

...

Because revenue is tied to inference spend on the platform rather than seat count or subscription tiers, sustaining revenue growth depends on token volume scaling faster than token unit prices decline. While inference costs dropped 1,000-fold between 2022 and 2024 and are projected to fall another 90% in per-token cost from 2025 to 2030, OpenRouter has scaled token consumption on the platform from 10 trillion tokens per year in June 2025 to over 100 trillion tokens per month as of August 2026. That volume growth is what positions OpenRouter for continued revenue growth despite falling per-token costs. Atallah has described inference as potentially “the largest market ever in software,” and OpenRouter’s take-rate model scales its revenue directly with that market’s growth.

...

In June 2025, OpenRouter announced it had raised a cumulative $40 million across a seed round and a Series A, at a $500 million Series A valuation, co-led by Andreessen Horowitz and Menlo Ventures, with Sequoia Capital and angel investors also participating. Beyond normalization, teams can define their own routing logic to determine how calls are distributed across different models.

OpenRouter takes a fundamentally different approach. It is a cloud-hosted API that developers call externally. There is no configuration, no infrastructure to manage, and no proxy to run.

OpenRouter offloads all of that. The tradeoff is routing flexibility. LiteLLM lets teams define fully custom routing criteria tailored to their system requirements. OpenRouter’s routing preferences are set at the model or provider level, meaning teams can either specify the model or model family they want to use, or optimize at the provider level based on price, performance, or security.
